title: What It Cost
year: c. 614–615 CE — the fourth and fifth years of prophethood
teaser: Quraysh held a meeting and agreed on torture. After that, a man with no clan paid with his body.

layers.title: The Meeting That Authorised It
layers.subtitle: A decision taken, not a mood that took hold
layers.content:
Al-Mubarakpuri is precise about the timing. For the first months of the open call, and into the beginning of the fourth year, Quraysh kept to insult, distortion and pressure. When it became clear that people were still entering Islam, they met again. At that meeting they approved something new: a campaign of torture, run tribe by tribe. Each leader would deal with the converts inside his own clan.

This matters. What followed was not a riot. It was policy, agreed in advance by men who governed a city and administered a sanctuary.

The method was calibrated to rank. Ibn Hisham describes Abu Jahl's approach: when a man of high birth converted, Abu Jahl would attack his judgement, mock his intelligence, and threaten his trade with ruin. When the convert was socially weak, he beat him without limit.

So the campaign fell along a single line — protection. A Makkan's safety was his clan's obligation. Kill a man with a clan and you owed his people blood. Break a slave, and you owed no one anything. Slaves, freed slaves, foreigners and the poor had nothing behind them, and they took nearly all of it.

The Prophet ﷺ himself was shielded, though imperfectly. His standing and character stayed the hands of many of his enemies, and behind him stood Abu Talib with a large and influential clan. That protection extended to him. It did not extend to Bilal.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 29:2 — 'Do people think they will be left alone because they say: we believe, and will not be tested?'
layers.source: Ibn Hisham 1/320, in Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar

layers.title: The Ones Without Clans
layers.subtitle: The sources keep their names
layers.content:
Bilal ibn Rabah belonged to Umayyah ibn Khalaf. When his master learned he had accepted Islam he beat him. Sometimes a rope was tied around his neck and the boys of the street were set to drag him through the alleys and over the hillocks of Makkah. Sometimes he was simply kept from food and water. Once he was bound in the valley in the hottest part of the day and a heavy stone laid on his chest, and Umayyah told him he would not stop until Bilal was dead or renounced Muhammad ﷺ and worshipped al-Lat and al-Uzza. Bilal said only: one, one. Abu Bakr passed by, and bought him, and freed him.

Ammar ibn Yasir, a freed slave of Bani Makhzum, was taken with his father and mother. All three were laid repeatedly on burning sand and beaten; Ammar at times was thrown onto embers. Yasir the father died of it. Sumayyah, his mother, was killed by Abu Jahl himself with a spear — al-Mubarakpuri records that she thereby became the first woman martyr in Islam. Ammar was worked on until, in a weak moment, he said a word that could be read as leaving the faith. He came straight to the Prophet ﷺ, who consoled him and confirmed his faith.

Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, owned by Umm Anmar, was seized by the hair and dragged, twisted by the neck, and thrown into fire; his tormentors pulled him back and forth across the embers until his back was burnt.

Abu Fakih Aflah was laid on scorching sand with a stone on his back so he could not move, and left until he lost consciousness. Abu Bakr purchased his freedom too.

Uthman ibn Affan's own uncle wrapped him in a mat of palm leaves and lit a fire beneath him. Mus'ab ibn Umair, raised in comfort, was starved by his mother and put out of her house.

Women were not exempt. Zanirah, an-Nahdiyah and her daughter, Umm Ubais and others are named. Among those who handled them, al-Mubarakpuri notes, was Umar ibn al-Khattab — before his own conversion.
layers.source: Ibn Hisham 1/317-320; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. III, 248-249; Usdul-Ghabah 1/591-592 — in Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar

layers.title: At the Ka'bah
layers.subtitle: The sanctuary gave him no cover either
layers.content:
The protection around the Prophet ﷺ held against killing. It did not hold against humiliation, and most of what is recorded happened in the sanctuary itself.

al-Bukhari narrates from Ibn Mas'ud that the Prophet ﷺ was praying near the Ka'bah while Abu Jahl sat nearby with his companions. One of them asked who would fetch the entrails of a slaughtered camel and put them on Muhammad's back while he prostrated. Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt went and got them, waited for the prostration, and laid them between his shoulders. They collapsed against each other laughing. The Prophet ﷺ stayed in prostration and did not lift his head until Fatimah came and took it off him. Ibn Mas'ud, watching, said he could do nothing and wished he had men with him.

When he raised his head he said three times: O Allah, destroy the Quraysh — and named them, Abu Jahl, Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, al-Walid ibn Utbah, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, and a seventh. Ibn Mas'ud ends the report by swearing that he later saw the bodies of those men in a well at Badr.

On another day, also in al-Bukhari, Uqbah put his cloak around the Prophet's neck while he prayed and twisted it hard. Abu Bakr came, caught the man by the shoulder and shoved him off, and said: do you kill a man because he says my Lord is Allah? In Asma's account of a similar day, they turned on Abu Bakr and beat him, and when they touched his hair afterwards it came away in their hands.

Abu Lahab pelted him with stones until his ankles bled. Umm Jamil scattered bundles of thorns on the paths he used. Neighbours threw the womb of a sheep at him while he prayed, and into his cooking pot.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Ablution and Book of Prayer, narrated by Ibn Mas'ud; and the chapter on what the pagans did to the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah
layers.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 1/37, 1/544; Ibn Hisham 1/416; Kanzul-Ummal 12/449 — in Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar

layers.title: The Verse for Ammar
layers.subtitle: What Allah settled about a man who broke
layers.content:
Only one of these events produced a ruling that is still applied today, and it came from the worst moment, not the best.

Ammar had said the words his torturers wanted. Nothing in his heart had moved, but his tongue had given way, and he came to the Prophet ﷺ knowing what he had done. Immediately afterwards the verse came down: «إِلَّا مَنْ أُكْرِهَ وَقَلْبُهُ مُطْمَئِنٌّ بِالْإِيمَانِ» — 'except him who is compelled, while his heart is at rest with faith.' (16:106)

Read the sentence carefully. It does not praise him and it does not excuse the words. It removes them from the account. The clause is an exception carved out of a verse about apostasy, and it draws the line at the place where the will stops: what is extracted by force is not counted as what a person chose.

That ruling is why Islamic law has, ever since, distinguished the coerced from the willing — in speech, in contracts, in confession, in divorce. It was not derived from a courtroom. It was derived from a man on burning sand.

The other divine response to these years was not a ruling but a record. The du'a at the Ka'bah named seven men. Ibn Mas'ud, who heard it, lived to see their corpses gathered at a well after Badr, and said so under oath. And what was said of the family of Yasir while they were still being beaten — be patient, your place is in the Garden — was not a rescue. It was information about where the account would be settled.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 16:106 — 'except him who is compelled, while his heart is at rest with faith'
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Ibn Mas'ud — the du'a against the seven and the bodies at the well of Badr
layers.source: Ibn Hisham 1/319-320; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. III, 248-249 — in Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar

layers.title: What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: Names on both sides of the ledger
layers.content:
Three things came out of these years.

The first is that wealth was given a use. Abu Bakr was among the few early believers with money, and what he did with it was buy people and let them go — Bilal, Amir ibn Fuhayrah, Abu Fakih and others. He did not fund a defence force. He bought the bodies the system claimed to own and returned them to their owners.

The second is a fixed point in the law. Because of Ammar, a Muslim under compulsion is not held to what compulsion produces. Whole schools of jurisprudence rest on that clause, and it exists because a man was pushed past what he could hold and the Qur'an took his side.

The third is the record itself. The sirah does not only preserve the names of the tortured; it preserves the names of the men who did it, the streets they used, and the phrasing of the threats. Umayyah ibn Khalaf. Abu Jahl. Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt. Uthman's uncle. Mus'ab's mother. Umar ibn al-Khattab, before his conversion. The sources make no attempt to soften any of it, including the fact that some of those hands later belonged to Muslims.

What a reader should carry is narrow and hard. Nobody in this chapter was rescued. The Prophet ﷺ walked past the family of Yasir and offered them the Garden because that was what he had to offer. Bilal was bought, not saved. Sumayyah died. And the community that came out of it was the one that could tell the difference between being protected and being right.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 2:214 — 'Or do you think you will enter Paradise before Allah tests those who came before you?'
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

quiz.prompt: According to al-Mubarakpuri, how did the campaign of torture begin?

options.text: Spontaneously, as mobs turned on converts in the streets
With a meeting at which Quraysh agreed on it, each leader handling his own tribe
By an order from the Byzantine governor of Syria
After the Muslims struck first at the Ka'bah

quiz.scholar_reflection: It was consultation, then policy, then execution. Insult and boycott had failed to stop conversions, so they escalated deliberately.

quiz.prompt: Who killed Sumayyah, the mother of Ammar ibn Yasir?

options.text: Umayyah ibn Khalaf
Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt
Abu Jahl, with a spear
Abu Lahab

quiz.citation: Ibn Hisham 1/319-320; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. III — Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Sealed Nectar records that she thereby merited the title of the first woman martyr in Islam. Her husband Yasir died of the same campaign.

quiz.prompt: What did Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt do while the Prophet ﷺ was in prostration near the Ka'bah?

options.text: Poured sand over his head
Placed the entrails of a slaughtered camel on his back
Struck him with a bow
Recited poetry to drown out his voice

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Ablution, narrated by Ibn Mas'ud
quiz.scholar_reflection: Abu Jahl's circle laughed until they fell against each other. The Prophet ﷺ did not lift his head from prostration until Fatimah came and removed it.

quiz.prompt: What did Abu Bakr say when he pulled Uqbah off the Prophet ﷺ, who was being strangled with his own cloak?

options.text: The Quraysh will answer for this
Do you kill a man because he says: my Lord is Allah?
Take me instead of him
He is under the protection of Abu Talib

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari 1/544, narrated by Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As
quiz.scholar_reflection: Asma reported that on a comparable day they turned on Abu Bakr and beat him, and afterwards his hair came away in the hand of anyone who touched it.

quiz.prompt: Which verse was revealed immediately after Ammar, under torture, uttered a word of disbelief?

options.text: 'Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity' (2:286)
'Except him who is compelled, while his heart is at rest with faith' (16:106)
'And be patient, for your patience is only by Allah' (16:127)
'Whoever kills a believer intentionally' (4:93)

quiz.scholar_reflection: The exception is carved out of a verse about apostasy. It removed his words from the account entirely, and became the basis in law for distinguishing the coerced from the willing.

quiz.prompt: The torture fell almost entirely on slaves, freed slaves and the poor, because they had no clan to demand blood for them. What do you make of a persecution shaped by who could be harmed without consequence?

options.text: It exposes the leaders as calculating rather than convinced — they harmed only where it was safe
It means the earliest sacrifices were made by the people with the least to gain
It shows a society where justice tracked lineage, which is precisely what the message dismantled
It is the ordinary pattern — the cost of any change is paid first by those least able to refuse

quiz.citation: Ibn Hisham 1/320 — Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: Abu Jahl threatened the trade of a rich convert and broke the body of a poor one. He knew exactly which he could get away with.

quiz.prompt: Ammar said the words. His heart did not change, but his tongue gave way, and revelation came down on his side. Where does that leave you with your own breaking point?

options.text: Relieved — Allah judges what a person chooses, not what is extracted from them
Sober — the verse covers compulsion, and most of what I concede is not compulsion
Struck that the Prophet ﷺ consoled him rather than corrected him
Aware that a limit is not a failure — everyone has one, and the Qur'an says so

quiz.slider_label: Mercy for weakness or a narrow exception
quiz.scholar_reflection: The clause is exact: compelled, and the heart at rest with faith. Both halves are required. It is a mercy with an edge on it.

quiz.prompt: The Prophet ﷺ did not intervene for Bilal, or for Khabbab, or for the family of Yasir. He was there, and he did not stop it. How do you hold that?

options.text: He had no power to stop it — his own protection ran only as far as Abu Talib's clan
Stopping it was never on offer; what he gave them was certainty about the outcome
Some trials are given precisely because no one can lift them
It is the hardest part of the chapter and I would rather it had gone differently

quiz.scholar_reflection: He was pelted until his ankles bled and choked in the sanctuary in front of witnesses. He was not standing above the persecution. He was inside it.

quiz.prompt: Abu Bakr's response to the torture was to spend his wealth buying slaves and setting them free. What does that tell you about what money is for?

options.text: He removed people from the system rather than fighting the system
It was the only form of protection available to him, and he used all of it
Wealth in the hands of a believer becomes an instrument, not a possession
He could not save everyone, and bought whom he could reach

quiz.citation: Ibn Hisham 1/317-318 — Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: Bilal, Amir ibn Fuhayrah, Abu Fakih and others. He was not raising an army with that money. He was buying people back.

quiz.prompt: The sources name the tormentors as carefully as the tormented — including Umar ibn al-Khattab, before his conversion. Why do you think Muslim historians preserved that?

options.text: Because a history that flatters its own heroes cannot be trusted about anything
Because the distance a person travels is part of what their faith means
Because the victims' testimony would be worth less if the record were edited
Because it leaves no one with the excuse that their past disqualifies them

quiz.citation: Ibn Hisham 1/319 — Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: The same books that record what Umar did to those women record him praying at the Ka'bah beside them two years later. Neither entry was removed.
